screens.title: The Decorator Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you'll learn a simple but powerful idea: instead of creating many subclasses to add features, you wrap objects with decorators that add behavior at runtime. We'll use a coffee-shop example where a plain coffee can be wrapped with milk, sugar, or whipped cream decorators. You'll see the core contract that keeps decorated and undecorated objects interchangeable, the abstract decorator that delegates work, and concrete decorators that add cost or description. This approach avoids an explosion of classes, reduces duplication, and keeps your system open to extension but closed to modification. We will also compare the Decorator to similar wrappers like Adapter and Proxy so you can avoid common confusions, and practice implementing decorators in Java using an abstract decorator and concrete wrappers. By the end you will be able to identify when Decorator fits, implement it to compose features at runtime, and reason about ordering and state interactions. Think about a feature you might want to toggle dynamically in your own code—Decorator is often a clean, composable way to do it.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Wrap objects with decorator instances that implement the same interface to add behavior flexibly at runtime.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Introduction
The Decorator Pattern
Enhancing objects dynamically without creating many subclasses.
In this lesson

You will learn the pattern's intent, its Java implementation using a common interface and abstract decorator, and real use cases such as Java I/O streams. Expect practical code examples and a hands-on text editor scenario.

Why it matters

Decorator keeps systems extensible without subclass combinatorics. It supports composition over inheritance so you can add or remove features at runtime.

Explore Key Topics
Pattern Intent
Attach responsibilities at runtime without changing interfaces.
Java Example
Implement Coffee and CoffeeDecorator to compose toppings.
Use Cases
I/O stream wrappers, logging, UI decorators, and feature toggles.
Visual concept
SimpleCoffee
base component: description + cost
MilkDecorator
SugarDecorator
WhippedCreamDecorator
Wrap to compose — no subclass for every combination

screens.title: Problem: Subclassing Explosion
screens.narratorSegment: Let's start with the problem the Decorator pattern solves: subclassing explosion. Suppose you have a basic Coffee class and three independent features: milk, sugar, and whipped cream. If you model each combination via inheritance, each new feature doubles the number of subclasses you need. You would create MilkCoffee, SugarCoffee, MilkSugarCoffee, WhippedCreamMilkSugarCoffee, and so on. This leads to many classes that duplicate logic, are hard to maintain, and make adding a new topping expensive. The pattern's claim is simple: composition scales where inheritance doesn't. Instead of encoding every combination in the type system, you keep one core component and attach features at runtime. A concrete example: a SimpleCoffee has description "Simple Coffee" and cost 2.0. If you add a MilkDecorator, you wrap the SimpleCoffee at runtime and adjust description and cost. A common misconception is that inheritance is always simpler; in small cases it might look simpler, but as soon as features multiply, inheritance yields rigid, brittle hierarchies. Key takeaway: when behavior needs to be combined in multiple independent ways, prefer runtime composition to avoid exponential subclass growth. Ask yourself: would adding a new topping force a new class for every existing combination?

keyIdea.title: Why this matters
keyIdea.text: Inheritance alone can create an unmanageable number of classes once features combine; decorators avoid that.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Subclassing Explosion
Definition

Subclassing explosion is the rapid growth of classes when each combination of independent features is modeled as a distinct subclass. It leads to duplication and inflexibility.

Concrete example
If you have three toppings, inheritance could require up to eight classes for all combinations. Maintaining shared behavior across those classes is error-prone and costly.
Analogy
Baking every cake flavor as a separate recipe file instead of layering ingredients before baking.
Common mistake
Using inheritance for independent features because it seems straightforward for the first one or two features.
Quick contrast
Inheritance encodes combinations at compile time. Decorators compose at runtime, so adding a feature is adding a wrapper, not a new leaf in the class tree.
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

When independent features must combine, prefer composition through decorators to avoid exponential subclassing.

screens.title: Decorator Pattern Explained
screens.narratorSegment: The Decorator pattern attaches additional responsibilities to an object dynamically while preserving its interface. At its heart are three roles: the component interface, the concrete component, and the decorator that also implements the component interface and holds a reference to a wrapped component. The decorator delegates calls and can add behavior before or after delegation. For example, the Coffee interface defines getDescription and getCost. SimpleCoffee implements those methods. CoffeeDecorator implements Coffee and stores a reference to another Coffee. A MilkDecorator extends CoffeeDecorator and augments getDescription by appending ", Milk" and getCost by adding 0.5. This keeps clients unaware of whether they have a plain or decorated coffee because all objects share the same interface. A misconception is that decorators change the object's type or break polymorphism — they do not. They preserve the component contract, enabling interchangeable usage. A good mental test: if you can treat a wrapped object exactly like the original via its interface, and decorators only change behavior, you have a correct design. Try composing three decorators and inspect the final description and total cost to confirm delegation.

keyIdea.title: Pattern summary
keyIdea.text: Decorators implement the same interface and hold a reference to a component, delegating and adding behavior without altering the contract.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Decorator Explained
Key roles
  • Component: common interface for operations like getDescription and getCost.
  • Concrete Component: the original object, e.g., SimpleCoffee.
  • Decorator: implements Component, wraps another Component, delegates, and adds behavior.
Misconception
Decorators do not change type or break polymorphism; they preserve the component interface so clients remain unaware of decoration.
Code example
<// Component interface
public interface Coffee {
  String getDescription();
  double getCost();
}
Concrete component
<// SimpleCoffee
public class SimpleCoffee implements Coffee {
  @Override
  public String getDescription() { return "Simple Coffee"; }
  @Override
  public double getCost() { return 2.0; }
}

screens.title: Abstract Decorator Structure
screens.narratorSegment: Let's inspect the abstract decorator that makes the pattern work. The abstract decorator implements the same component interface and holds a protected reference to another component. By delegating to that reference, the decorator can preserve default behavior and selectively extend methods. For example, CoffeeDecorator implements Coffee and stores a decoratedCoffee field. Its getDescription and getCost delegate to decoratedCoffee by default. Concrete decorators extend this abstract class and override only what they change — MilkDecorator appends ", Milk" to the description and adds 0.5 to the cost. This layering is recursive: a decorator can wrap either a concrete component or another decorator. The architecture ensures minimal code duplication because the abstract decorator centralizes the delegation logic. A subtle pitfall is exposing mutable state through decorators; if multiple decorators modify shared state, ordering matters and unexpected interactions can occur. When implementing, keep decorators small and focused. A quick test: trace calls through a wrapped stack to confirm each decorator invokes the wrapped object's method and then applies its enhancement. That trace helps diagnose ordering issues and unintended side effects. Abstract Decorator Structure means the abstract decorator centralizes delegation so concrete decorators can add behavior without duplicating forwarding logic.. In practical terms, how the decorator delegates to its component. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: The abstract decorator centralizes delegation so concrete decorators can add behavior without duplicating forwarding logic.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Abstract Decorator
Structure
The abstract decorator implements the component interface and maintains a reference to a component. It delegates calls to that reference by default so concrete decorators need only add their enhancements.
Example code
<// Abstract Decorator
public abstract class CoffeeDecorator implements Coffee {
  protected Coffee decoratedCoffee;
  public CoffeeDecorator(Coffee decoratedCoffee) { this.decoratedCoffee = decoratedCoffee; }
  @Override public String getDescription() { return decoratedCoffee.getDescription(); }
  @Override public double getCost() { return decoratedCoffee.getCost(); }
}
Design notes
  • Delegation centralizes forwarding logic and reduces duplication.
  • Concrete decorators override only methods they augment.
  • Decorators may be stacked recursively; trace calls to debug order issues.
Pro tip
Pro Tip

Keep decorators focused and stateless when possible. If decorators hold state, document how order affects behavior.

screens.title: Concrete Decorators: Milk, Sugar, Whipped Cream
screens.narratorSegment: Concrete decorators are small classes that extend the abstract decorator and add specific responsibilities. In the coffee example, MilkDecorator appends ", Milk" to the description and adds 0.5 to cost. SugarDecorator appends ", Sugar" and adds 0.2. WhippedCreamDecorator adds ", Whipped Cream" and 0.7. Because each decorator delegates to the wrapped component, you can stack them in any order to produce combined behavior. For example, wrapping SimpleCoffee with SugarDecorator, then WhippedCreamDecorator, then MilkDecorator produces a final description listing all three toppings and a cost equal to the base plus each decorator's surcharge. A practical detail: description order reflects wrapping order; cost is additive and typically independent of order. A common misconception is that decorators must be expensive objects; they should be lightweight and stateless unless necessary. When implementing, keep methods concise and let the abstract decorator handle delegation. The concrete decorators demonstrate the pattern's benefit: adding features by writing a tiny wrapper instead of creating a new subclass for each feature combination. Concrete Decorators: Milk, Sugar, Whipped Cream means each concrete decorator adds a single responsibility, keeping additions modular and composable.. In practical terms, implementing specific behavior in wrappers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Concrete Decorators
MilkDecorator
<// Milk Decorator
public class MilkDecorator extends CoffeeDecorator {
  public MilkDecorator(Coffee decoratedCoffee) { super(decoratedCoffee); }
  @Override public String getDescription() { return decoratedCoffee.getDescription() + ", Milk"; }
  @Override public double getCost() { return decoratedCoffee.getCost() + 0.5; }
}
Sugar & Whipped Cream
<// Sugar Decorator
public class SugarDecorator extends CoffeeDecorator { /* ... +", Sugar" and +0.2 */ }

<// Whipped Cream Decorator
public class WhippedCreamDecorator extends CoffeeDecorator { /* ... +", Whipped Cream" and +0.7 */ }
Example usage
Compose decorators at runtime to form new combinations without subclassing.
Example card
SimpleCoffee wrapped by MilkDecorator yields "Simple Coffee, Milk" and cost 2.5.
Common mistake
Making decorators heavy with unrelated responsibilities instead of one focused enhancement.
Key takeaway
Concrete decorators are small, focused wrappers that compose features at runtime.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Client Usage
Client example
<// Client code
public class CoffeeShop {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    Coffee myCoffee = new SimpleCoffee();
    System.out.println("Order 1: " + myCoffee.getDescription() + " | Cost: $" + myCoffee.getCost());

    // Add Milk
    myCoffee = new MilkDecorator(myCoffee);
    System.out.println("Order 2: " + myCoffee.getDescription() + " | Cost: $" + myCoffee.getCost());

    // Fancy coffee with multiple decorators
    Coffee fancyCoffee = new SimpleCoffee();
    fancyCoffee = new SugarDecorator(fancyCoffee);
    fancyCoffee = new WhippedCreamDecorator(fancyCoffee);
    fancyCoffee = new MilkDecorator(fancyCoffee);
    System.out.println("Order 3: " + fancyCoffee.getDescription() + " | Cost: $" + fancyCoffee.getCost());
  }
}
Notes & checks
  • Declared type is Coffee; runtime object is decorated stack.
  • Order of wrapping affects description order; cost is additive in this example.
  • Wrapping the same reference updates the object in place for that variable.
Check your understanding
Exercise

Construct two separate decorated coffees and verify their descriptions and costs are independent.

screens.title: Decorator vs Inheritance, Adapter, Proxy
screens.narratorSegment: Decorators are object wrappers, and that sometimes causes confusion with Adapter and Proxy. The key difference lies in intent. Decorator's intent is to add responsibilities to an object without changing its interface. Adapter's intent is to change an interface so a class can be used where a different interface is expected. Proxy's intent is to control access to an object, maybe adding lazy initialization, access checks, or caching. A practical example: wrapping a FileInputStream with a BufferedInputStream is a decorator because buffering adds behavior while preserving the InputStream interface. Using an adapter would be appropriate if you needed to present a completely different A P I to clients. A common misuse is to implement a decorator that alters the contract unexpectedly, effectively behaving like an adapter; that breaks substitutability. Another misconception is thinking a proxy always adds security. While proxies often do, their main role is access control or surrogate behavior. When identifying which pattern to apply, ask: am I adding behavior while preserving the interface (Decorator), changing the interface (Adapter), or controlling access (Proxy)? That simple question clarifies intent and prevents design drift.

keyIdea.text: Decorator preserves the interface and adds behavior; Adapter changes the interface; Proxy controls access.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Pattern Comparison
Decorator vs Inheritance
Decorator composes features at runtime and avoids subclass explosion; inheritance encodes combinations in types and can become unmanageable when features combine independently.
Decorator vs Adapter vs Proxy
  • Decorator: add responsibilities, preserve interface.
  • Adapter: change interface so code can interoperate.
  • Proxy: control access, add surrogates like caching or security.
Examples
Java I/O streams use decorators (BufferedInputStream) to add behavior. An adapter would be used if you needed to present a different API, and a proxy might manage access to a resource.
Check
Ask which intent matches your case: add behavior, change interface, or control access?

screens.title: Java I/O Streams: A Classic Decorator
screens.narratorSegment: A canonical real-world example of the Decorator pattern is Java's input and output stream classes. FileInputStream provides raw byte input. You can wrap it with BufferedInputStream to add buffering, and then with DataInputStream to provide methods for reading primitive data types. Each wrapper implements the same InputStream or FilterInputStream interface and delegates calls to the wrapped stream, adding behavior such as buffering or data conversion. Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Hands-on: Editor
Starter code (excerpt)
<// Component interface
interface TextEditor {
  String getContent();
  String render();
}

<// Concrete Component
class BasicTextEditor implements TextEditor {
  private String content;
  public BasicTextEditor(String content) { this.content = content; }
  @Override public String getContent() { return content; }
  @Override public String render() { return "Plain Text: " + content; }
}

<// Abstract Decorator
abstract class TextEditorDecorator implements TextEditor {
  protected TextEditor decoratedEditor;
  public TextEditorDecorator(TextEditor decoratedEditor) { this.decoratedEditor = decoratedEditor; }
  @Override public String getContent() { return decoratedEditor.getContent(); }
  @Override public String render() { return decoratedEditor.render(); }
}

screens.title: Common Pitfalls and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Decorators are powerful, but they come with pitfalls. First, creating too many fine-grained decorators can make the object graph hard to understand; prefer meaningful, composable decorators rather than dozens of micro-wrappers. Second, decorators that hold or mutate shared state can introduce ordering-dependent bugs. If multiple decorators update the same underlying field, the sequence of wrapping can change behavior unexpectedly. Third, if a decorator changes the external contract or throws new exceptions, substitutability breaks and clients may fail. Best practices: keep decorators focused and stateless when possible, centralize delegation in an abstract decorator, and document any ordering or state constraints. When debugging, trace the call chain through wrappers to see where values are transformed. A helpful pattern is to write small unit tests for a few typical decorator stacks to catch interaction problems early. Finally, measure whether decorators improve clarity compared to a simple utility function or composition approach; use the pattern where runtime composition and per-instance behavior are true requirements. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the chapter's essential concepts. First, the Decorator Pattern: a structural pattern that attaches behavior to an individual object at runtime without affecting other objects of the same class. These three items form the foundation of decorator design and help you recognize where to apply the pattern in real systems. fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you'll learn a simple but powerful idea: instead of creating many subclasses to add features, you wrap objects with decorators that add behavior at runtime. We'll use a coffee-shop example where a plain coffee can be wrapped with milk, sugar, or whipped cream decorators. You'll see the core contract that keeps decorated and undecorated objects interchangeable, the abstract decorator that delegates work, and concrete decorators that add cost or description. This approach avoids an explosion of classes, reduces duplication, and keeps your system open to extension but closed to modification. We will also compare the Decorator to similar wrappers like Adapter and Proxy so you can avoid common confusions, and practice implementing decorators in Java using an abstract decorator and concrete wrappers. By the end you will be able to identify when Decorator fits, implement it to compose features at runtime, and reason about ordering and state interactions. Think about a feature you might want to toggle dynamically in your own code—Decorator is often a clean, composable way to do it.

In this first objectives view, we set learning targets you will reach by studying the Decorator pattern. First, you will be able to explain the pattern's intent and benefits: that is, why wrapping objects avoids subclass combinatorics and supports composition over inheritance. For example, in a coffee shop app you will describe how adding milk or sugar becomes a matter of wrapping rather than creating new classes. Second, you will learn to distinguish Decorator from inheritance. We will show concrete contrasts so you can spot when subclassing creates brittle hierarchies and when composition with decorators offers flexibility. Each objective ties a conceptual skill to a practical outcome, so you won't just name the pattern — you'll explain when it helps. Finally, pay attention to the micro-mnemonics on these cards; they map objectives to small implementation checks you can use when reviewing code. By the end of this screen's objectives you should already be thinking about places in your code where runtime composition would simplify design.

This second objectives view ties each learning outcome to a practical check you can perform in code reviews or exercises. For explaining intent, show an example where multiple features compose without a new subclass per combination; the coffee example is ideal because milk and sugar compose naturally. To differentiate from inheritance, point to a small subclass tree that would explode when features combine, and contrast it with a decorator composition that stays small. For implementation, your proof is working Java code: a Coffee interface, a SimpleCoffee concrete component, an abstract CoffeeDecorator that delegates by default, and concrete decorators that override methods to add description and cost. Finally, for scenario identification, practice mapping real features—logging, buffering, UI styling—to decorators and explain why runtime composition matters. Each card includes a verified competency milestone so you can self-audit. Use these checks when you finish exercises and during pair programming: can you add a new feature by writing a decorator rather than a subclass?

Let's start with the problem the Decorator pattern solves: subclassing explosion. Suppose you have a basic Coffee class and three independent features: milk, sugar, and whipped cream. If you model each combination via inheritance, each new feature doubles the number of subclasses you need. You would create MilkCoffee, SugarCoffee, MilkSugarCoffee, WhippedCreamMilkSugarCoffee, and so on. This leads to many classes that duplicate logic, are hard to maintain, and make adding a new topping expensive. The pattern's claim is simple: composition scales where inheritance doesn't. Instead of encoding every combination in the type system, you keep one core component and attach features at runtime. A concrete example: a SimpleCoffee has description "Simple Coffee" and cost 2.0. If you add a MilkDecorator, you wrap the SimpleCoffee at runtime and adjust description and cost. A common misconception is that inheritance is always simpler; in small cases it might look simpler, but as soon as features multiply, inheritance yields rigid, brittle hierarchies. Key takeaway: when behavior needs to be combined in multiple independent ways, prefer runtime composition to avoid exponential subclass growth. Ask yourself: would adding a new topping force a new class for every existing combination?

The Decorator pattern attaches additional responsibilities to an object dynamically while preserving its interface. At its heart are three roles: the component interface, the concrete component, and the decorator that also implements the component interface and holds a reference to a wrapped component. The decorator delegates calls and can add behavior before or after delegation. For example, the Coffee interface defines getDescription and getCost. SimpleCoffee implements those methods. CoffeeDecorator implements Coffee and stores a reference to another Coffee. A MilkDecorator extends CoffeeDecorator and augments getDescription by appending ", Milk" and getCost by adding 0.5. This keeps clients unaware of whether they have a plain or decorated coffee because all objects share the same interface. A misconception is that decorators change the object's type or break polymorphism — they do not. They preserve the component contract, enabling interchangeable usage. A good mental test: if you can treat a wrapped object exactly like the original via its interface, and decorators only change behavior, you have a correct design. Try composing three decorators and inspect the final description and total cost to confirm delegation.

Let's inspect the abstract decorator that makes the pattern work. The abstract decorator implements the same component interface and holds a protected reference to another component. By delegating to that reference, the decorator can preserve default behavior and selectively extend methods. For example, CoffeeDecorator implements Coffee and stores a decoratedCoffee field. Its getDescription and getCost delegate to decoratedCoffee by default. Concrete decorators extend this abstract class and override only what they change — MilkDecorator appends ", Milk" to the description and adds 0.5 to the cost. This layering is recursive: a decorator can wrap either a concrete component or another decorator. The architecture ensures minimal code duplication because the abstract decorator centralizes the delegation logic. A subtle pitfall is exposing mutable state through decorators; if multiple decorators modify shared state, ordering matters and unexpected interactions can occur. When implementing, keep decorators small and focused. A quick test: trace calls through a wrapped stack to confirm each decorator invokes the wrapped object's method and then applies its enhancement. That trace helps diagnose ordering issues and unintended side effects. Abstract Decorator Structure means the abstract decorator centralizes delegation so concrete decorators can add behavior without duplicating forwarding logic.. In practical terms, how the decorator delegates to its component. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Concrete decorators are small classes that extend the abstract decorator and add specific responsibilities. In the coffee example, MilkDecorator appends ", Milk" to the description and adds 0.5 to cost. SugarDecorator appends ", Sugar" and adds 0.2. WhippedCreamDecorator adds ", Whipped Cream" and 0.7. Because each decorator delegates to the wrapped component, you can stack them in any order to produce combined behavior. For example, wrapping SimpleCoffee with SugarDecorator, then WhippedCreamDecorator, then MilkDecorator produces a final description listing all three toppings and a cost equal to the base plus each decorator's surcharge. A practical detail: description order reflects wrapping order; cost is additive and typically independent of order. A common misconception is that decorators must be expensive objects; they should be lightweight and stateless unless necessary. When implementing, keep methods concise and let the abstract decorator handle delegation. The concrete decorators demonstrate the pattern's benefit: adding features by writing a tiny wrapper instead of creating a new subclass for each feature combination. Concrete Decorators: Milk, Sugar, Whipped Cream means each concrete decorator adds a single responsibility, keeping additions modular and composable.. In practical terms, implementing specific behavior in wrappers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Now we'll walk through client code that composes decorated objects. Start with a SimpleCoffee instance which implements Coffee. Then assign it to a variable and wrap that variable with a MilkDecorator to add milk. You can continue to wrap the same reference or create a new variable for a different combination. The code sequence shows how the getDescription call on the final object returns a concatenation of all decorator descriptions and getCost returns the base cost plus each decorator's surcharge. A concrete example from the source: printing order states after each decoration illustrates how wrapping changes runtime behavior without altering original classes. A common misconception is that wrapping must produce new types; in reality the declared type remains the component interface. Another pitfall: when decorators access mutable state of the wrapped component, order can affect results. Always test combinations to ensure decorations interact as intended. Try constructing two different decorated instances to confirm that each composition is independent and that wrapping is a cheap runtime operation. Client Usage: Building Orders means clients construct decorated objects by wrapping components; results are observed through the shared interface.. In practical terms, progressively wrapping objects in client code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Decorators are object wrappers, and that sometimes causes confusion with Adapter and Proxy. The key difference lies in intent. Decorator's intent is to add responsibilities to an object without changing its interface. Adapter's intent is to change an interface so a class can be used where a different interface is expected. Proxy's intent is to control access to an object, maybe adding lazy initialization, access checks, or caching. A practical example: wrapping a FileInputStream with a BufferedInputStream is a decorator because buffering adds behavior while preserving the InputStream interface. Using an adapter would be appropriate if you needed to present a completely different A P I to clients. A common misuse is to implement a decorator that alters the contract unexpectedly, effectively behaving like an adapter; that breaks substitutability. Another misconception is thinking a proxy always adds security. While proxies often do, their main role is access control or surrogate behavior. When identifying which pattern to apply, ask: am I adding behavior while preserving the interface (Decorator), changing the interface (Adapter), or controlling access (Proxy)? That simple question clarifies intent and prevents design drift.

A canonical real-world example of the Decorator pattern is Java's input and output stream classes. FileInputStream provides raw byte input. You can wrap it with BufferedInputStream to add buffering, and then with DataInputStream to provide methods for reading primitive data types. Each wrapper implements the same InputStream or FilterInputStream interface and delegates calls to the wrapped stream, adding behavior such as buffering or data conversion. This layering illustrates the pattern's strengths: you can add buffering, then conversion, then higher-level parsing as separate wrappers without changing the underlying FileInputStream. A common misunderstanding is to think these wrappers change the underlying stream type; they present compatible interfaces so client code can call the same methods. When you design your decorators, model the Java input and output approach: keep wrappers focused, delegating most work, and only add the small enhancement the wrapper is responsible for. Observing this example in the JDK helps ground the pattern in code you may already use every day. In practical terms, how java composes stream behaviors via wrappers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Decorators are powerful, but they come with pitfalls. First, creating too many fine-grained decorators can make the object graph hard to understand; prefer meaningful, composable decorators rather than dozens of micro-wrappers. Second, decorators that hold or mutate shared state can introduce ordering-dependent bugs. If multiple decorators update the same underlying field, the sequence of wrapping can change behavior unexpectedly. Third, if a decorator changes the external contract or throws new exceptions, substitutability breaks and clients may fail. Best practices: keep decorators focused and stateless when possible, centralize delegation in an abstract decorator, and document any ordering or state constraints. When debugging, trace the call chain through wrappers to see where values are transformed. A helpful pattern is to write small unit tests for a few typical decorator stacks to catch interaction problems early. Finally, measure whether decorators improve clarity compared to a simple utility function or composition approach; use the pattern where runtime composition and per-instance behavior are true requirements. Let's summarize the chapter's essential concepts. First, the Decorator Pattern: a structural pattern that attaches behavior to an individual object at runtime without affecting other objects of the same class. It provides a flexible alternative to subclassing by favoring composition. Second, the Component: the common interface or abstract class that both concrete components and decorators implement so decorated objects remain interchangeable. Third, the Concrete Component: the original object to which behavior can be attached, like SimpleCoffee. These three items form the foundation of decorator design and help you recognize where to apply the pattern in real systems. Continuing the summary, these three cards capture the remaining essentials. A Decorator is an abstract wrapper that implements the component interface and delegates to a wrapped component. Concrete Decorators extend that abstract wrapper to add specific responsibilities, like MilkDecorator or SpellCheckDecorator. Dynamic Responsibility refers to the pattern's ability to add or remove features at runtime instead of at compile time through subclassing. Remember: decorators preserve the interface, delegate by default, and add focused behavior. That combination makes them ideal for composing orthogonal features such as formatting, logging, and buffering while keeping the codebase open for extension.
